chunks: From him, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a debt of one hundred kurrs of dates owed to him by another, and the debtor has a date palm grove; so the creditor comes to him and says, 'Give me your palm grove in exchange for what is owed to me,' as if the Imam disliked this.

And I asked him about a man who has a debt of loads of fresh dates or dried dates owed to him by another; so he sends to him to collect it, but the debtor becomes unable to pay, so he sends him dinars and says, 'Buy with these and complete the remainder of what is owed to you.'
He said, 'There is no harm in this if he trusts him.'

key_terms.ائْتَمَنَهُ: If he trusts him / with mutual trust
key_terms.كُرٍّ: A traditional unit of volume measurement for dry goods

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pay a debt of dates with money or property in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the permissibility of *sufaha* (exchange of debt for goods) in Shia jurisprudence, specifically addressing the conversion of commodity debts (dates) into real estate (palm groves) or currency (dinars). Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates these transactions provided there is mutual trust (*i'timad*) and agreement, distinguishing them from prohibited *riba* (usury) by ensuring the exchange settles an existing obligation rather than creating a new speculative one. This ruling underscores the flexibility in commercial contracts when the underlying asset is already owed, a key principle in resolving debt disputes in early Islamic markets.
